text:
Docker Fixes Critical Two-Year-Old Hub Flaw That Let One User Push Images as AnotherSwati KhandelwalOct 13, 2026

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it.

The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it.

The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account.

Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4.

The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install.

Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner.

Each personal access token acts as the account that owns it, at a permission level chosen when the token is created. While the flaw was open, conversion changed the owner recorded for each token and left its secret unchanged.

An attacker could abuse this by creating a token on an account they controlled, converting that account into an organization, and naming another user as its owner. The token would then work at the registry as that user.

The named owner was not asked to confirm the change and was not notified, according to Docker and the researchers who reported the flaw. Docker's conversion page has included the sentence "The new owner receives a notification email" since at least August 2024.

Within the token's permission level, a transferred token could pull, push, or delete images in the named owner's repositories and in organizations the owner could access.

Docker rated the flaw critical because that access "includes publishing images under a legitimate name," it said.

In March and April, attackers used stolen publisher credentials to push malicious Trivy images and malicious KICS images to the publishers' own Docker Hub repositories, according to Docker.

Peter Molnar and Krisztian Hozak of mptrdev.com found the flaw and reported it to Docker, which says it deployed the fix less than four hours after receiving their report. They named the flaw GhostPat.

In their technical write-up, the two say they reproduced the flaw twice on consenting test accounts. They logged in to the registry as the target account, created and pushed to a repository in its namespace, pushed to an organization it belonged to, and pulled its private repositories.

What Docker's Review Covered

Docker reviewed every account conversion made while the flaw was open and compared them with registry logs and token records. It looked for any token used under more than one identity and examined every push made with a transferred token, about 304,000 in all.

"We found no evidence that the vulnerability was exploited," the company said.

Every one of those pushes went to a repository belonging to the converted organization or to its named owner, according to Docker. In the large majority of cases, both accounts belonged to the same person or team.

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

An attacker chained three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure, a VPN appliance, to run commands as root without logging in, security firm Volexity said on October 13. Ivanti has released fixes for two of the flaws and told customers on affected versions to "act immediately." A fix for the third is still pending, according to Volexity.

Volexity, which reported the flaws to Ivanti, found the attack on one customer's appliance. The appliance was fully patched at the time and running version 22.8R2.4. The attacker, which Volexity tracks as UTA0576, began exploiting it on October 3.

Ivanti said on October 13 that it is aware of "limited exploitation in the wild."

The first two flaws are an authentication bypass and a remote code execution flaw, tracked together as CVE-2026-104935. Together they let an attacker run code as the appliance's cgi-server user, and the third flaw, a privilege escalation, raises that to root, Volexity said.

The CVE record Ivanti filed shows which Connect Secure versions are affected:

Affected: Connect Secure "before version 25.1.3.0"
Not affected: version 22.7R2.14 "or prior"
Listed as unaffected: versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1

Ivanti's security advisory has more on the affected versions and the fixes.

The release notes for 25.1.3.0 are dated July 2026. Customers already on that version are outside the range the CVE record gives.

Ivanti is working on a fix for the privilege escalation flaw, which will come "in a future release in the coming weeks," Volexity said. Its report does not say what risk that flaw carries on an appliance where the first two are fixed.

Ivanti tells customers to upgrade and to run its Integrity Checker Tool regularly. That tool misses this chain, Volexity said, because the exploit changes library code only in memory and restores the configuration data it alters. The attacker also took steps to stay hidden from the tool.

Confirming a compromise takes forensic investigation, including network and memory forensics, according to Volexity. These signs come from the one incident it investigated:

URL path: /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi, requested in large numbers
HTTP header: X-DSCGI-PATH on those requests, with a value that does not match the URL path
Directory: /data/.icscap/
IP: 108.165.147[.]64, the host the attacker used

In that incident, the attacker stole stored credentials, including LDAP domain credentials, searched Active Directory for passwords, and ran password-spraying attacks against its accounts. No backdoor or web shell was left behind. The attacker reran the entire exploit chain for each command.

Volexity's report and Ivanti's post do not name a temporary workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet. They also do not say whether upgrading removes access an attacker has already gained.

Volexity assessed with low confidence that UTA0576's motive is criminal, not espionage. Neither company said how many customers were attacked.

Ivanti rates CVE-2026-104935 8.6 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale. In its own entry in the CVE record, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) marks exploitation as "active" and the technical impact as "total."

Separately, the same Ivanti post covers fixes for two other products, Xtraction and Neurons Patch for Intune, and Ivanti said it is not aware of those flaws being exploited. Each has a flaw Ivanti rates 9.9 out of 10: CVE-2026-106042 in Xtraction before version 2026.4, and CVE-2026-109412 in Neurons Patch for Intune.

A flaw in SAP's Cloud SDK for Python can send an application's OAuth2 client credentials to a server an attacker controls, SAP said in a security advisory on October 13. The flaw affects multi-tenant applications on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) that use the SDK, SAP's official Python client for BTP services. An attacker must be able to control the tenant subdomain, the name such an application passes to the SDK to say which tenant a request is for.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-89111 and carries SAP's CVSS score of 10.0 out of 10. The advisory names version 0.45.2, released on August 21, as the fix.

The SDK handles authentication for those services with the application's client credentials, a client ID and a client secret. Version 0.45.2 added a check that rejects any tenant subdomain that is not a simple name.

Six later releases do not apply that check in every case, The Hacker News found. Versions 0.53.0 through 0.55.0, published between September 10 and September 18, skip it when an application calls the SDK's Destination service module.

Version 0.53.0 moved that module onto new shared code for requesting tokens, and that code did not include the check. Version 0.55.1 added it there on September 18.

Passing a tenant subdomain that contains URL delimiters "now raises ValueError immediately instead of silently routing credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint," the 0.55.1 release notes say.

The Hacker News ran SAP's own tests for the check on October 13, against the source code of every release from 0.45.1 to 0.58.4 and of the three 0.36 releases. The six releases failed 9 of the 11 tests SAP added with version 0.55.1. That version and the 11 releases after it passed all 11.

As of October 13, the advisory lists no version above 0.45.2 as affected. Neither it nor the release notes say whether the six releases fall under CVE-2026-89111.

Two releases on the older 0.36 line also lack the check. Versions 0.36.1 and 0.36.2 were published on September 4 and September 10, after the August fix, and failed the tests SAP wrote for it. Both fall inside the advisory's range of versions below 0.45.2.

Releases

Tenant subdomain check

Basis

Below 0.45.2, including 0.36.1 and 0.36.2

Missing

SAP advisory. The Hacker News test of 0.36.0, 0.36.1, 0.36.2 and 0.45.1.

0.45.2 to 0.52.2

Present

The Hacker News test of all 18 releases.

0.53.0 to 0.55.0

Missing for Destination calls. Also missing for Document Management Service calls in 0.55.0.

SAP's 0.55.1 release notes. The Hacker News test of all 6 releases.

0.55.1 to 0.58.4

Present

The Hacker News test of all 12 releases.

What to Do

Versions 0.45.2 through 0.52.2 and 0.55.1 through 0.58.4 contain the check. Version 0.58.4 was the newest release on PyPI, the Python package index, on October 13.

Upgrading within the 0.36 line does not add the check. None of its three releases contains it.

Applications that cannot upgrade yet can compare each tenant subdomain with a list of their registered tenants before passing it to the SDK, SAP says in the advisory.

The flaw matters only where an application passes a tenant subdomain to the SDK. The August fix covered three modules: Agent Gateway, Destination and Document Management Service.

The advisory does not say whether applications that ran a release without the check should replace their client credentials.

How the Flaw Works

dinsdag 13 oktober 2026, 17:01 door Redactie, 0 reacties

Ivanti waarschuwt klanten voor actief misbruik van een kwetsbaarheid in Ivanti Connect Secure vpn-servers. Via het beveiligingslek (CVE-2026-104935) kan een ongeauthenticeerde aanvaller willekeurige commando's op de server uitvoeren. Het probleem is een 'authentication bypass', maar verdere details worden niet gegeven. Ivanti roept klanten op om de beschikbaar gestelde update naar versies 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, 25.1.3.1 of 22.8R2.5 zo snel mogelijk te installeren en de Integrity Checker Tool te draaien.

Ivanti Connect Secure, eerder nog bekend als Pulse Secure, is een vpn-oplossing waarmee gebruikers toegang tot het netwerk van hun organisatie kunnen krijgen. Volgens Ivanti is een 'beperkt aantal klanten' getroffen waarmee direct wordt samengewerkt. Om hoeveel klanten het precies gaat wordt niet gemeld. Verder laat het bedrijf weten dat er op dit moment geen betrouwbare Indicators of Compromise (IoC's) zijn waarmee organisaties kunnen controleren of hun vpn-server is gehackt. Klanten die een hack vermoeden wordt geadviseerd herstelmaatregelen uit te voeren.

Daarnaast meldt Ivanti dat het 'een gedeelte van deze kwetsbaarheid' al in juli had gepatcht. "We waren bezig met het backporten van de fix naar andere ondersteunde versies toen misbruik plaatsvond", zo laat het bedrijf verder weten. Producten van Ivanti zijn geregeld het doelwit van aanvallen. Het Amerikaanse cyberagentschap is bekend met 36 verschillende kwetsbaarheden die bij aanvallen zijn ingezet.

Franse overheid adviseert supermarkten om koelsystemen offline te halen

dinsdag 13 oktober 2026, 13:42 door Redactie, 3 reacties

De Franse overheid adviseert supermarkten en andere bedrijven om hun koelsystemen offline te halen. In het geval van gehackte koelinstallaties wordt aangeraden om een fabrieksreset uit te voeren. Volgens het Franse Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) is in Frankrijk een groot aantal koelsystemen van de Deense fabrikant Danfoss gehackt.

Het CERT-FR stelt dat het niet verstandig is om de admin-interface van deze koelsystemen toegankelijk te maken vanaf het internet. In het geval remote beheer toch nodig is wordt aangeraden om toegang tot vertrouwde ip-adressen te beperken. In het geval van een gehackt koelsysteem adviseert de Franse overheidsdienst om netwerktoegang alleen toe te staan voor de leverancier. Verder is een fabrieksreset vereist, moeten alle beveiligingsupdates worden geïnstalleerd, alle gebruikte secrets worden gewijzigd en moeten supermarkten de aanwezige accounts controleren.

De Britse beveiligingsonderzoeker Kevin Beaumont merkt op dat de genoemde update het 'datum-gebaseerde backdoor-wachtwoord' verwijdert. Eerder meldde Beaumont dat duizenden Danfoss-koelsystemen die op internet toegankelijk zijn gebruikmaken van een wachtwoord dat op de huidige datum is gebaseerd. Cybersecuritybedrijf Aviatrix stelt dat de aanvallers die bij honderden Franse supermarkten de temperatuur van de koeling verhoogden twee kwetsbaarheden combineerden, CVE-2025-41450 en CVE-2025-41451.

CVE-2025-41450 betreft een 'authentication bypass' waarvoor vorig jaar maart al een update van Danfoss verscheen. Onderzoekers van cybersecuritybedrijf Claroty noemden dit ook het "code-of-the-day" inlogmechanisme, waarbij het mogelijk is om via een datum-gebaseerd wachtwoord in te loggen. In augustus publiceerden de onderzoekers een analyse van dit beveiligingslek en hoe het te gebruiken is om koelsystemen aan te vallen.

Attackers took remote control of fridges and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets on the night of October 11 and warmed them, forcing stores to throw food away, several retail chains said.

The attackers reached them through the controller that runs all of a store's fridges and freezers, a device made by Danish company Danfoss that maintenance firms can manage remotely. Les Mousquetaires, which owns the Intermarché chain, said its fridges and freezers were put into defrost and heated to as much as 50°C.

CERT-FR, the French government's computer emergency response team, said in an alert published in French on October 12 that it is aware of numerous compromises affecting two Danfoss controller series, the AK-SM and the AK-SC. It told operators to disconnect the controllers or filter access to them.

CERT-FR is part of ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. ANSSI's head, Vincent Strubel, called it urgent to take the two series off the internet or filter access very tightly, AFP reported.

Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has so far said who carried out the attack or how the attackers got into the controllers. Danfoss said most of the units hit were older models that it no longer updates.

Which Chains Were Hit

The chains gave their own figures to AFP, Reuters and broadcaster RTL. Each counts the stores the attack reached.

A store on that list did not always lose its stock. Schelcher told RTL that the cold chain held in most of the 80 Coopérative U stores hit, and that only a minority could not react fast enough and lost goods, according to AFP. He praised the quick reaction of store staff and refrigeration contractors.

Intermarché, by contrast, said its affected stores had to throw away all the products concerned.

Thierry Cotillard, who heads Les Mousquetaires, told broadcaster BFMTV he expected losses of tens of millions of euros across France, according to Reuters.

In its statements on October 12, Danfoss gave no figure for how many systems were hit. It told Reuters it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems."

Which Controllers, and Whether They Can Be Patched

Danfoss told AFP that most of the units hit were older products that no longer get software or security updates, and it named two: the AK-SM 800 and the AK-SC 355.

Danfoss declared the AK-SM 800 end-of-life in May 2021 and phased out the AK-SC 355 in 2016. In an October 2025 newsletter, it said it would end all services for such older products and urged customers to plan replacements.

Some units of the current model, the AK-SM 800A, were also hit. Those were running outdated firmware, according to Danfoss's statement to trade publication Cooling Post, which did not name the versions.

Two of 31 newly disclosed flaws in Progress Software's MarkLogic Server database could let an account given only some management privileges take administrator control of the server, the company says.

Progress published all 31 on October 12 and scored five of them critical. Fixes have been available since September 10, in MarkLogic 11.3.7 and MarkLogic 12.1.0.

Affected releases, and the release that fixes each:

MarkLogic 11.x before 11.3.7: upgrade to 11.3.7
MarkLogic 12.x before 12.1.0: upgrade to 12.1.0

MarkLogic 11.3 is the long-term support (LTS) line. The 12 line, which Progress calls an innovation release, has no patched 12.0 release. Its fix is 12.1.0, which also adds new features.

Installing the fixes for the 10 MarkLogic flaws Progress disclosed in August is not enough. Those fixes arrived in 11.3.6 and 12.0.3, and both releases are affected by the new flaws.

Progress's CVE records and its upgrade notes for the two releases do not say whether any of the 31 flaws has been used in attacks. None was in the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog when The Hacker News checked on October 13.

The same records and notes list no workaround for customers who cannot upgrade yet.

What the Critical Flaws Allow

Progress scored three of the five critical flaws 9.9 out of 10 on the CVSS scale and the other two 9.6. For each one, the attacker must already have a privilege or a way to run code on the server, according to the company's CVE records.

Two of them involve forests. In MarkLogic, a forest is a collection of documents that is attached to a database.

The fix for CVE-2026-85947 shows which accounts are at issue. A "forest-scoped administrative grant" is no longer enough on its own to attach a forest to a database of the account's choosing, the upgrade notes say. They also tell customers to review delegated forest and database privilege assignments before upgrading, and to audit the roles that hold xdmp-eval-in.

Outside researchers reported four of the five through Bugcrowd. A researcher using the handle rexnets is credited with CVE-2026-85947, CVE-2026-85948, and CVE-2026-85956, and another using the handle WaltWhitehat is credited with CVE-2026-9191.

Flaws That Depend on Configuration

Progress scored 24 of the remaining flaws high and two medium. The highest, CVE-2026-85954, at 8.6, could allow an attacker to gain more privileges than granted by passing values to certain XQuery functions.

When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM

October 13, 2026

TL;DR;

Our security assessment of LiteLLM (v1.77.7), a widely used open-source LLM gateway, uncovered multiple high-impact vulnerabilities (tracked as CVE-2026-35029, CVE-2026-59823) which have been resolved as of LiteLLM version 1.83.9.

The most significant issues stemmed from a missing authorization check on the /config/update endpoint, which allowed any authenticated user (including low-privileged accounts) to modify the proxy’s runtime configuration. This single flaw enabled arbitrary file read, administrative account takeover, and remote code execution via malicious Python modules loaded from cloud storage. A separate SSRF vulnerability in the “Clientside LLM Credentials” feature allowed attackers to redirect API calls and exfiltrate provider keys. These findings highlight that as AI infrastructure tools rapidly evolve, foundational security practices like proper access control and input validation remain essential.

Introduction

As LLM gateways see wider adoption, understanding the security risks they introduce is essential to deploying them safely within an AI stack. These systems sit between applications and model providers and often handle credentials, configuration, and request routing. We decided to take a closer look at LiteLLM, one of the most popular LLM gateways in use today. What started as an exploratory review uncovered multiple high severity vulnerabilities, including credential extraction, access control bypass, and remote code execution. This post presents our findings and highlights the security pitfalls that can arise in LLM gateway deployments and the wider LLM ecosystem.

What are LLM Gateways?

LLM gateways are systems that sit between an application and one or more LLM providers. Instead of calling model APIs directly, applications route requests through a gateway, which then forwards those requests to the appropriate model backend.

In practice, LLM gateways are often used to centralize concerns such as provider abstraction, credential management, request routing, rate limiting, logging, and usage tracking. Many gateways also add higher level features like fallback logic, load balancing across providers, and configuration driven model selection.

LiteLLM

LiteLLM is an open-source project that provides an SDK and a gateway product for working with multiple LLM providers. The project originated through Y Combinator and is widely used across the LLM ecosystem.

In this post, we focus exclusively on the LiteLLM gateway. The gateway is commonly deployed as a standalone service and plays a central role in how LLM requests are handled in many LLM-based applications. Its widespread adoption and position in the request path made it a suitable target for our research.

Our review of LiteLLM was conducted against version 1.77.7. The sections below outline the defects we discovered in the LiteLLM gateway.

Access Control Bypass in /config Endpoint

The LiteLLM proxy exposes an administrative endpoint ‘POST /config/update’, designed to allow runtime modifications to the proxy configuration. This endpoint facilitates updating critical settings, including environment variables, model lists, and general proxy settings.

The Vulnerability

The vulnerability stems from a missing role-based access control (RBAC) check within the endpoint’s implementation, combined with an overly permissive route allowlist for UI sessions.

1. Missing Function-Level Authorization

In secure administrative endpoints within LiteLLM (e.g., /invitation/new), the code explicitly verifies that the authenticated user possesses the PROXY_ADMIN role before proceeding.

title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.
Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).
At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.
Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.
Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

New Proofpoint-Ponemon Institute report finds nearly three in four U.S. healthcare organizations experienced disruption to patient care due to cyberattacks

SUNNYVALE, Calif.– October 13, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, and Ponemon Institute, a top IT security research organization, today released findings from their fifth annual Cyber Insecurity in Healthcare report, revealing that cyberattacks are increasing in frequency, cost, and operational impact across U.S. healthcare organizations.

97% of organizations surveyed experienced at least one cyberattack in the past 12 months, of which 74% reported disruption to patient care as a result. AI adoption is also outpacing governance, with AI agents operating without guardrails emerging as a leading cause of data loss, cited by 24% of respondents.

“Cyber resilience has become essential to healthcare resilience,” said Ryan Kalember, chief strategy officer, Proofpoint. “When a cyberattack delays a procedure, extends a hospital stay, or forces patients to another facility, cyber risk becomes patient risk. AI is now adding another dimension as people and AI systems access the same sensitive data and clinical workflows. Healthcare organizations need security built around those interactions so they can adopt AI without compromising the trust patient care depends on.”

This year’s report, based on responses from 705 IT and IT security practitioners at U.S. healthcare organizations, highlights several trends:

Operational disruption is becoming healthcare’s biggest cyber cost

title: Malware Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) | Recorded Future
text:
PUBLISHED ON 13 OCT 2026

Recorded Future

One malware hash can turn a vague alert into a concrete investigation. Analysts can search endpoints for the exact file, trace where it appeared, and determine whether related activity exists elsewhere. But if the attacker changes the file, the hash changes too. Domains and Internet Protocol (IP) addresses can also lose relevance as attackers rotate infrastructure.This is why malware indicators of compromise work best as evidence within a larger investigation, not as isolated entries on a blocklist. Their value grows when analysts can establish where an indicator came from, how recently it was observed, what threats are connected to it, and whether those connections matter to their organization.Malware indicators of compromise are technical artifacts or observations that suggest malicious activity. They help security teams detect, investigate, and contain threats, but an IoC is most useful when analysts can assess its source, timing, confidence, and relationship to other threat activity.Key takeaways
Malware indicators can include file-based artifacts, network infrastructure, and other technical evidence associated with malicious activity.
IoCs do not exclusively describe past attacks. They can point to malicious activity that may be underway or has already occurred.
Indicator types have different defensive lifespans. An IP address may quickly lose relevance, while a file hash remains an exact identifier for the same sample even if attackers create a new version.
Threat intelligence can add context that helps analysts prioritize IoCs, connect related activity, and move from an isolated match toward a wider investigation.
What are malware indicators of compromise?An indicator of compromise (IoC) is a technical artifact or observable that suggests malicious activity. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines IoCs broadly enough to include signs that an attack may be imminent, underway, or that a compromise may already have occurred.For a security operations center (SOC) analyst or incident responder, an IoC can help answer a practical question: Have we seen evidence associated with this threat in our environment?Analysts can use malware IoCs to validate an alert, search logs and endpoints for related activity, or scope an incident after malicious activity is confirmed. They can also use an indicator as a starting point for investigating connected infrastructure, malware, or attacker behavior.An IoC does not automatically prove that an organization has been compromised. Context matters. Finding a malware hash executing on an endpoint carries a different meaning from finding the same hash in an intelligence feed.IoCs and TTPs serve different purposesIndicators of compromise identify observable evidence associated with malicious activity. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) describe how an adversary operates.A specific command-and-control domain is an IoC. The techniques an attacker repeatedly uses to establish persistence or move through a network are TTPs.Atomic indicators are often easier to match against security telemetry, but attackers may be able to change them quickly. TTP-based detection can be harder to evade when it focuses on established attacker behavior, but it can also demand richer telemetry and more detection engineering.Security teams do not need to choose one or the other. An IoC can provide the first concrete lead, while TTPs can help analysts search for related activity after an attacker changes a domain or recompiles malware.The most common types of malware indicatorsMalware indicators generally appear either in files and host activity or in network communications. Each gives analysts a different view of what the malware has done.File-based IoCsFile hashes such as SHA-256 fingerprints allow security tools to identify an exact known file. U.S. CISA ADDS IVANTI CONNECT SECURE FLAW TO ITS KNOWN EXPLOITED VULNERABILITIES CATALOG
Pierluigi Paganini

October 13, 2026
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Ivanti Connect Secure flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added an Ivanti Connect Secure FortiMail flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score of 8.6), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The vulnerability is an authentication bypass issue caused by spoofing in ICS versions before 25.1.3.0 that could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. ICS versions 22.7R2.14 and earlier are not affected.

“Authentication bypass by spoofing in ICS before version 25.1.3.0 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. This does not impact ICS version 22.7R2.14 or prior.” reads the advisory. “Ivanti has released updates for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) which addresses one high severity vulnerability. Successful exploitation could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.”

The company confirmed that the vulnerability was exploited in attacks in the wild.

“We are aware of exploitation in the wild affecting a limited number of customers at the time of disclosure.” continues the report.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by October 16, 2026.

ANTHROPIC SHOWS HOW SMALL AI MODELS COULD REPLICATE ACROSS IOT DEVICES
Pierluigi Paganini

October 13, 2026
Anthropic researchers show how small AI models could autonomously replicate across IoT devices, raising concerns about adaptive, AI-powered botnets.

Anthropic published a paper this week that should make anyone who manages IoT infrastructure sit down for a moment. The research shows that small AI models are approaching the capability to replicate themselves autonomously across networks of cheap, poorly secured devices, the kind of Android TV boxes that sell for fifty dollars on Amazon.

The team ran a 26 billion parameter model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed across 15 off-brand Android TV boxes networked together. It worked. The boxes collectively ran inference at 0.39 tokens per second, slow by any normal standard, but functional, and that’s the point.

The researchers broke autonomous replication into four steps: finding devices on a network, gaining access, setting up the AI model on a new device, and repeating the process. Previous studies had already shown that small models can handle many of the hacking tasks involved. This paper looks at a different question: can a model work out how to run itself on unfamiliar hardware? That’s a key ability for an AI worm that can spread across different devices.

A model with 9 billion parameters successfully set up inference on 8 of the 9 hardware types tested. Models with 30 billion parameters or fewer can already handle many of the individual steps needed for replication, although they still struggle to complete the entire process without errors. In the tests, only one model, GLM-5.2, reliably completed the full process from scratch. It spread to all 8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials.

Pierluigi Paganini

October 13, 2026
Hackers hit French supermarkets via unpatched Danfoss refrigeration systems, remote-heating freezers and destroying stock worth millions.

Overnight from Sunday to Monday, a large cyberattack hit the refrigeration systems of hundreds of French supermarkets, BFMTV revealed. The attackers targeted equipment from the Danish maker Danfoss that many French stores use to regulate their cold. Fresh and frozen stock was destroyed, and the Paris prosecutor says there were also fires.

The method is simple and nasty. Refrigeration systems have a forced defrost function that clears ice buildup, and the attackers appear to have triggered it remotely in a continuous mode, with a temperature setting of 50 degrees. The equipment heated for several hours instead of keeping goods cold, and when staff opened the fridges and freezers in the morning, a sector source told BFM, “a wave of heat” came out.

“300 Intermarché and Netto stores, and fewer than 100 U stores, were affected on Monday, October 12, by a cyberattack targeting the refrigeration control systems of the Danish manufacturer Danfoss, according to the two retailers.” reports BFMTV. “Hackers reportedly remotely altered the temperatures of the systems, causing the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products.”

The scale is still being counted. The Mousquetaires group says 300 of its Intermarché and Netto stores were affected, Coopérative U says fewer than a hundred of its outlets, and E.Leclerc confirmed repercussions on cooling equipment in several stores without giving numbers. title: CVE-2026-97229: Critical GitLab RCE Flaw Enables Unauthenticated Code Execution
text:
GitLab has released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-97229, a maximum-severity remote code execution vulnerability affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). The flaw has a CVSS score of 10.0 and could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable GitLab server under certain conditions.

The vulnerability resides in GitLab’s CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler and results from insufficient validation of specially crafted regular expressions. Successful exploitation could compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of a GitLab environment without requiring authentication or user interaction.

GitLab released patched versions 19.2.8, 19.3.4, and 19.4.2 on October 12, 2026, strongly urging administrators of self-managed installations to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com already runs the fixed release, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take additional action.

With source-code management and CI/CD infrastructure containing sensitive repositories, credentials, deployment secrets, and access to production environments, vulnerabilities in GitLab can create significant risks for modern software supply chains.

Security teams can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, accelerating threat hunting and detection engineering while adapting detection logic to their organization’s security telemetry.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-97229 Analysis

CVE-2026-97229 affects GitLab CE and EE installations across three currently vulnerable release branches:

GitLab 19.2 before 19.2.8

GitLab 19.3 before 19.3.4

GitLab 19.4 before 19.4.2

The vulnerability is caused by an integer overflow in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler. This component processes regular expressions used within project pipeline configurations. According to GitLab, insufficient regular expression validation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to supply a specially crafted expression that ultimately results in arbitrary code execution on the GitLab server.

GitLab assigned the vulnerability the maximum CVSS 3.1 score of 10.0, with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. This reflects the severity of a network-accessible vulnerability that requires neither authentication nor user interaction and can potentially have a high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

The flaw is particularly dangerous because GitLab servers commonly occupy a highly privileged position within development infrastructure. They can host proprietary source code, CI/CD variables, deployment credentials, access tokens, configuration files, and integrations with cloud and production environments.

Arbitrary code execution on the underlying GitLab server could therefore provide attackers with opportunities to access sensitive repositories, extract secrets, manipulate source code, interfere with pipelines, establish persistence, or use compromised infrastructure as a stepping stone toward additional systems.

The vulnerability was reported to GitLab through its HackerOne bug bounty program by security researcher joaxcar. GitLab has not publicly specified the exact date on which the issue was initially discovered or privately reported. It was publicly disclosed with the October 12, 2026 critical patch release.

The disclosure follows other recent vulnerabilities affecting GitLab’s regular expression processing components. In September 2026, GitLab patched CVE-2026-93577, another integer overflow in the Regular Expression Compiler, as well as CVE-2026-89078, a double-free vulnerability in the Regular Expression Parser. Those earlier flaws required authentication, whereas the newly disclosed vulnerability can be triggered by an unauthenticated attacker under the conditions described by GitLab.

The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk

When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.
While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

Internal Reconnaissance: A High-Volume, Noisy CampaignThe intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.Authentication Abuse and Documentation BrowsingThe pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.Early Detection, Containment, and RemediationIn the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.What This Investigation RevealedThis case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. title: Employee Arrested After Listening Device Found in OpenAI Conference Room, FBI and the Company Say
text:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden in the conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a camera at the time it was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on a half-dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device was installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also he also used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left an unattended bag in a different room in the building that included his wallet, identification and another recording device.

title: Agent Baseline Publishes Security Reference Architecture for Software Factories
text: BackSecurity NewsAgent Baseline Publishes Security Reference Architecture for Software FactoriesAgent Baseline’s new reference architecture shows how to secure software factories with four boundaries enforced outside the AI agent.Sarah GoodingOct 13, 2026|2 min read Agents now write a large share of the code at some of the biggest engineering organizations. Uber says more than 70% of its pull requests are attributed to local or cloud agents, and its weekly agent requests grew 9.4 times between February and August. Stripe’s internal coding agents, which it calls Minions, write more than a thousand of the pull requests Stripe merges each week, and engineers can start one from a Slack message. Vercel’s factory for maintaining its AI SDK authored 25 to 35% of the pull requests merged to main each week during its first four weeks. These systems, which the industry has started calling software factories, take work from a prompt, a ticket, or an alert and carry it through to tested code, and the most advanced ones deploy and operate what they build.Every agent in those systems makes decisions a developer used to make: which commands to run, which packages to install, and which services to call. Most security models still assume a person is making those calls. Agent Baseline today published The Secure Software Factory: A Reference Architecture, which lays out how to secure a factory when the agent itself can’t be relied on to stay within its limits. Socket CTO Ahmad Nassri co-authored it with contributors from Docker, Keycard, Barclays, and Secure Theory. The paper opens with the PocketOS incident from April, in which a coding agent on a routine staging task found an API token in an unrelated file and used it to delete the company’s production database, along with the backups stored with it, in nine seconds. The reference architecture treats the agent as untrusted and enforces its limits from outside its decision loop.Four boundaries, covering the sandbox the agent runs in, the network it can reach, the supply chain it draws from, and the identity and access it acts under, are held by infrastructure the agent can’t configure or reach. The agent proposes, policy authorizes, and infrastructure enforces. The numbers mark the four boundaries: 1 sandbox, 2 network, 3 supply chain, 4 identity and access. Figure from The Secure Software Factory: A Reference Architecture, Agent Baseline, CC BY 4.0.The paper applies those boundaries at three levels of autonomy, from a developer directing a single coding agent, to a predefined workflow running the factory as a shared service, to an orchestrator agent that decides what work happens next. The boundaries stay the same at every level, and the infrastructure takes on more of the supervision people used to do as the factory becomes more autonomous.Socket focuses on the supply chain boundary, which limits agents to the components and sources the organization has approved. Packages, dependencies, and models that enter during a run have to come through an admission point, such as a registry or a supply chain firewall, that serves approved versions and hides unsafe ones so a goal-seeking agent doesn’t go looking for them.Ahmad described the behavior behind that requirement on the Insecure Agents podcast, where he explained that agents denied a package have gone to the CDN for the tarball, rewritten the registry configuration, or run their own DNS lookups to reach npm or PyPI directly. In the Secure Software Factory reference architecture, an egress proxy that the agent can’t reconfigure closes off those routes, since all of the agent’s traffic passes through it and it allows only approved destinations.Version 1 of the paper is available at agentbaseline.org/reference-architecture and is open for comment on GitHub.

Technical Analysis
The vulnerability resides in the put_file function of the jailexec connection plugin. In an Ansible architecture, a connection plugin is responsible for moving files to and executing commands on a managed node. For the FreeBSD Jail Connection Plugin, the managed node is a FreeBSD jail accessed via jexec. When put_file is invoked, the plugin resolves a transfer's destination to a path on the jail host — a path that is outside the jail's namespace — and then runs mkdir -p and mv at that location with root privileges on the host.
The core flaw is a classic link-following issue (CWE-59, Improper Link Resolution Before File Access). The mkdir -p and mv commands operate on the host-side path, and neither operation protects against symbolic links. If an attacker has already placed a symlink inside the jail at or above the destination path used by the Ansible task, the host-side, root-privileged mv will follow the symlink and write the file to the symlink's target on the host. Because the path is operated on outside the jail, the symlink effectively redirects the root-owned write to any location on the host filesystem writable by root.
The attack surface is the normal file-transfer workflow of the plugin. The precondition is twofold: the operator must run a task that uses put_file (e.g., copy, template, or fetch), and the attacker must be able to create a symlink inside the jail at or above the task's destination before the transfer executes. The jail's root, or any process with write access to a directory an Ansible task will later target, satisfies the attacker capability requirement.

title: Ivanti Zero-Day Chain Gave Attackers Root Access to Fully Patched VPN
text:
Ivanti on Tuesday warned customers that a zero-day vulnerability in its Connect Secure (ICS) VPN appliances has been exploited in the wild.

Tracked as CVE-2026-104935 and rated high severity, the issue is an authentication bypass that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti says it’s aware of exploitation affecting a limited number of customers.

Volexity discovered the in-the-wild exploitation while investigating an incident at one of its customers. A previously undocumented threat actor it tracks as UTA0576 had chained three zero-days to gain unauthenticated, root-level code execution on a fully patched ICS appliance.

According to Volexity, CVE-2026-104935 covers two of the flaws: an authentication bypass and a remote code execution bug. Ivanti has patched these vulnerabilities with the release of ICS versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1.

The third vulnerability, a privilege escalation issue, remains unpatched, and the vendor plans to fix it over the coming weeks.

Volexity, which found evidence of exploitation starting on October 3, says UTA0576 focused primarily on credential theft, data exfiltration, network reconnaissance, and log tampering.

The attackers stole domain credentials stored on the appliance and exfiltrated limited Active Directory metadata. Using a custom tool, they searched Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

They also ran password-spraying attacks, tested credentials with a custom Kerberos tool, and tried to extract credentials from captured network traffic. They also scanned the network, collected the appliance’s configuration data, and parsed authentication logs to identify valid usernames. Volexity found no backdoor or web shell on the device.

The operation was detected and disrupted before the attackers’ ultimate goals became clear. Volexity believes with high confidence that their actions pointed to preparation for lateral movement and a wider compromise of the network.

“Volexity assesses with low confidence that UTA0576 has criminal, rather than espionage, motivations based on the target of this activity,” the company says.

“As with many other threat actor operations Volexity has investigated in 2026, Volexity assesses with medium confidence that UTA0576 makes use of large language models (LLMs) for exploit development and post-exploitation activity,” it added.

ASTRO was assessed as a Rust-based command and control framework intended for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Capabilities were identified across remote command execution, credential access, persistence, reconnaissance, lateral movement, and anti-forensics. Production readiness across all supported operating systems should therefore not be inferred from the number of available commands. Additional intelligence value was identified in the operator authentication imple- mentation, deployment manifests, traffic profiles, domain generation logic, and migration documentation.

The company disclosed the incident to SecurityWeek, the same day notifications began going out.

Meta has not said what kinds of personal information were involved. It did say that a large share of the records that appeared to be personal data were actually synthetic or anonymized test data. As a result, the attackers may not be able to easily tell real records apart from fake ones.

That data included a small amount of personal information about a limited number of people, most of whom were employees.

The Housing Ombudsman Service says the incident has been contained and investigations are ongoing; the central outstanding fact is whether personal information was affected. While the watchdog works with its external supplier and has alerted the ICO, residents and leaseholders are left to rely on phone and email routes for new complaints and to exercise caution against potential scams. Written by

Several retail firms across Europe have confirmed cyber incidents that are causing operational disruptions.

On October 12, Netherlands-based multinational retail company Ahold Delhaize confirmed it was experiencing “a security issue” within its networks and had to take “some systems offline” to protect them.

The disruption was reported to affect three of the group’s brands, including supermarket chain Albert Heijn, operating in the Netherlands and Belgium, Dutch drugstore chain Etos and Dutch liquor store chain Gall & Gall.

The next day, Reuters reported that South African retail group The Foschini Group (TFG), owner of high-street fashion brands Hobbs and Whistles, was investigating a “cyber incident.”

The press agency said TFG became aware of an incident on October 11 affecting its UK subsidiary TFG London, with “certain IT systems” impacted.

Specifically, it was reported that the affected brands include Phase Eight and Hobbs and Whistles brands.

The South African group added there is “no reason to believe that payment information is at risk” at this stage. Other TFG high street brands, including Inside Story and White Stuff, are not affected.  The group’s TFG Africa and TFG Australia subsidiaries are also not experiencing any operational disruption.

TFG said it had reported the incident to the relevant UK authorities.

Commenting on this TFG incident, Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, noted, “The fact that Inside Story and White Stuff within the same group were unaffected, and that TFG’s wider Africa and Australia operations were untouched, suggests some degree of system separation was in place. That separation, which limited the blast radius, is worth noting as a positive.”

Additionally, according to The Times, H&M is also examining information circulating online about a potential incident.

However, at the time of writing, the retailer said it had found no indication that its data environment had been compromised.

There is currently no indication that these incidents are in any way related to each other.

ASOS Confirms Scope of Cyber-Attack

The incidents come days after customers of UK fashion retailer ASOS received a strange push notification indicating the company was hacked.

While the firm confirmed the unauthorized intrusion into “third-party platforms” it uses to communicate with customers and that personal information including names and contact details and some non-personal account related information “have been accessed,” it reiterated, in its latest customer update, published on October 13, that no payment-card information or account passwords were impacted.

The latest alerts also come as many supermarket chains in France are still dealing with a large-scale cyber-attack where attackers tampered with refrigeration controlling systems in the night between October 11 and 12, leading to the loss of a large amount of food products and financial losses estimated in hundreds of thousands of euros.

Daiichi Kosho, a major Japanese entertainment company and operator of the popular Big Echo karaoke chain, has revealed a significant data security incident. The breach occurred not on Daiichi Kosho's systems, but at a third-party supplier, Nippon Columbia Group (NCG), which manages customer data for the company. A malware infection on an NCG employee's computer may have resulted in the exposure of personal information belonging to 8,724,000 customers. The incident serves as a stark reminder of the critical importance of supply chain security and vendor risk management.
Threat Overview
The breach was discovered after NCG identified a malware infection on an employee's computer between October 1 and October 2, 2026. An investigation revealed that a file containing customer data from Daiichi Kosho was temporarily stored on this compromised device. While NCG isolated the PC, they could not rule out the possibility that the data was exfiltrated by the threat actor behind the malware. NCG notified Daiichi Kosho of the potential leak on October 5. The attack vector was a classic supply chain compromise, where the defenses of a primary company are bypassed by targeting a weaker link in its network of partners.
Technical Analysis
The root cause of the incident was a malware infection on a single endpoint within the supplier's network. The initial vector for the malware infection was not specified in the reports, but common methods include:

Phishing: The employee may have been tricked into opening a malicious attachment or clicking a link in a phishing email (T1566 - Phishing).
Malicious Download: The employee might have downloaded the malware from a compromised website or untrusted source.

Once active on the PC, the malware likely performed data discovery to find sensitive files (T1005 - Data from Local System) and then exfiltrated the customer data file to an attacker-controlled server (T1041 - Exfiltration Over C2 Channel).
Impact Assessment
The breach may have exposed a significant amount of personally identifiable information (PII) for over 8.7 million individuals. The compromised data includes:

Customer names
Genders
Dates of birth
Email addresses
Telephone numbers

Fortunately, passwords and credit card information were not affected. The primary risk to the affected customers is an increased likelihood of targeted phishing campaigns, social engineering, and identity theft. For Daiichi Kosho, the incident carries significant reputational damage and potential regulatory scrutiny, even though its own systems were not breached. It underscores the principle that a company is ultimately responsible for the security of the data it collects, regardless of where it is stored or processed.

Written by

Phil MuncasterUK / EMEA News Reporter, Infosecurity MagazineEmail PhilFollow @philmuncaster

One of Japan’s biggest karaoke box operators has revealed a data breach at a supplier which it claims may have exposed personal information of over eight million customers.

Daiichi Kosho has several popular brands including Big Echo, one of the country’s largest karaoke box chains, and also manufactures karaoke entertainment systems.

It published a statement on October 8 claiming an incident at Nippon Columbia Group (NCG), a Japanese entertainment group which handles customer information for the firm.

“According to NCG, between October 1 and October 2, 2026, a malware infection was discovered on one of their employees' devices (a PC), and the device was isolated from the network on October 2. Following an investigation into the scope of the impact by NCG, we received a report from NCG on October 5,” it explained.

“Personal data related to work outsourced to us was temporarily stored on the device in question, and we cannot rule out the possibility that this data may have been leaked.”

Read more on data breaches: KDDI Breach Affects Six Japanese ISPs, Exposes 14.2 Email Credentials.

NCG has reset affected passwords and is investigating the cause of the incident as well as whether data was compromised or not, the notice continued.

“Based on the information we currently have, approximately 8,724,000 customers who registered or made reservations at our stores may have had their names (registered names), genders, dates of birth, email addresses, and telephone numbers leaked to external parties,” it warned.

Daiichi Kosho urged customers to be on the lookout for possible phishing attempts using this personal information.

“Please be extremely careful of suspicious emails, SMS messages and phone calls, and do not open any links or attachments that you do not recognize,” it said. “We will never ask you for your password or credit card information. We ask for your continued caution.”

The majority of those impacted by the potential breach are customers of Big Echo (5.6 million) and the company’s DK Dining brands (3.5 million). Other affected businesses include Mega Big, Banana Club, Karaoke Club Dam and B-Garage.

Daiichi Kosho has opened a toll-free number for any concerned customers to get in touch while it confirms what happened.

Japan in the Crosshairs of Cyber-Attacks

The news comes after several cyber-attacks in recent weeks that have rocked the country.

In September, two major railway operators in the Tokyo region revealed separate incidents. Subway operator Tokyo Metro said an unauthorized third party had accessed the email addresses of 59,000 passengers signed up to its Metpo loyalty scheme.

At around the same time, Keio Corporation revealed a ransomware attack, although it’s not clear whether any data was compromised.

Car-rental company Times Car announced on September 25 that an unauthorized third party gained access to its website, leading to the compromise of personal information on 6.6 million members and former members.

Last year a major ransomware attack on food and beverage giant Asahi Group Holdings severely disrupted operations.

Japan has long been playing catch up on cybersecurity, due partly to chronic skills shortages and poor governance.

A new Active Cyber Defence law which came into force on October 1 will empower the Self Defense Forces (SDF) and police to proactively access and neutralize hostile foreign servers, but it may do little to improve cybersecurity posture in regular organizations, especially SMBs.

On October 5, 2026, Danish authorities announced a major data breach of the Denmark Central Person Register (CPR), the national population database. The incident exposed the personal data of approximately 8.8 million individuals, including current and former residents. The attackers did not exploit a technical vulnerability but instead abused the legitimate access credentials of a trusted third-party company. For about 10 days, the threat actors executed a high volume of automated queries to exfiltrate names, addresses, and the unique 10-digit CPR identification numbers. The data breach occurred in September 2026 when an unidentified threat actor gained control over and misused the account of a private Danish company. This company had legitimate, authorized access to query the CPR system. Instead of hacking the CPR directly, the attackers leveraged this trusted relationship to harvest data at scale. This method is often referred to as a supply chain or third-party attack, where the target's security is circumvented by compromising a less secure partner.
The attackers performed a large number of automated queries over approximately 10 days, a pattern of activity that was flagged as unusual by the register's administration on October 2, 2026. The compromised data includes:

Full Names
Addresses

The attack vector was the abuse of legitimate credentials, a form of T1078 - Valid Accounts. The attackers specifically exploited a T1199 - Trusted Relationship between the Danish government and the private company. The core of the data exfiltration was a 'smash and grab' operation using automated scripts to make a high volume of queries. This suggests the attackers focused on data collection rather than persistence or lateral movement within the CPR system itself.
The detection of the breach was based on anomaly detection, specifically the unusual surge in query volume from the compromised company's account. This highlights the importance of monitoring the behavior of even trusted, authorized users.
Impact Assessment
This is a highly significant data breach with severe potential consequences for the 8.8 million affected individuals. The CPR number is a national identification number in Denmark, used for nearly all interactions with public authorities and many private services like banking, healthcare, and insurance. The exposure of this number alongside names and addresses creates a critical risk of:

Identity Theft and Fraud: Criminals can use the data to impersonate individuals, open fraudulent accounts, or apply for loans.

Since the European Commission announced its intention to revive the project of an internal market for defence, Member States have been on alert. The issue is particularly sensitive. Using the EU budget to strengthen the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB) is one thing, regulating defence markets — and public procurement in particular — is quite another. Some countries are supportive, others remain sceptical, while others are still weighing up what position to take.

The idea of an internal market for defence does, after all, raise major issues. This is no longer simply a matter of supporting industry: it touches on the very exercise of national sovereignty, as governments decide which weapons and military equipment their security will ultimately depend on.

These questions have therefore been the subject of intense debate within the EU institutions for several months. In Brussels, even the terminology remains contested: a Defence Single Market? An Internal Market for Defence? A Defence Equipment Market?

But what is the view from European capitals? How are these issues perceived at national level? And what positions do the main Member States intend to defend in Brussels? To answer these questions, the ARES Group asked nine of its researchers, based in nine EU capitals, to examine the debate from their respective national perspectives. The picture that emerges is a nuanced one. National positions certainly diverge, but they are far from set in stone, and several areas of convergence are beginning to emerge. More importantly, some of these disagreements appear to stem from misunderstandings that could be clarified, potentially opening the way to compromise.

When it comes to protecting voice calls, security professionals typically focus on the security of the data carrying the audio — above all on encryption. Sooner or later though, the voice data stops being a stream of bits and becomes an analog signal that goes straight to the speakers. You might think that if someone is using headphones, nobody can listen in. But headphones are electronic devices, and their components have physical characteristics that can give away closely guarded secrets without any cyberattack at all. In a recent paper, researchers from two Hong Kong universities came up with InjectEave — an attack that exploits these properties to intercept the already-decoded analog audio signal.
How the InjectEave attack works
The electronic components in headphones convert data into analog form and amplify the signal to drive the speakers. This process generates weak electromagnetic emissions. Capturing those emissions and extracting information from them is a field unto itself, with many experts working in it. The main issue those experts face lies in the fact that stray emissions from headphones are too faint to intercept and analyze in practice.
The authors of InjectEave propose adding a radio transmitter that beams a signal at a specific frequency toward the target device. Those weak emissions from the headphones’ analog components modulate the transmitter’s signal. The altered signal can be intercepted from several meters away — provided the receiving antenna is sensitive enough. The attacker then analyzes the changes in the signal to reconstruct the original audio.
Technical details of the InjectEave attack
The main obstacle to intercepting electromagnetic emissions directly — without an external transmitter — is the relatively low signal frequency. For example, the audio amplifier in headphones operates at frequencies from 20Hz to 20kHz. By contrast, electromagnetic emissions are easiest to intercept at frequencies measured in megahertz. The researchers were able to find a transmitter frequency that would also “amplify” the low-frequency signal of interest.
The researchers ran a series of experiments. They used antennas to transmit the “amplifying” signal and receive the result, and a spectrum analyzer to capture and process the data. The authors have posted the raw recordings of the intercepted signals on a dedicated microsite, so anyone can check how well the attack works. In most cases, getting a usable result didn’t even require complex processing or recognition. Conversations picked up from wireless headphones are clearly intelligible despite the elevated noise level.
In total, the authors tested three models of wireless headphones and two models of basic wired headsets. The effective eavesdropping distance varied from one to six meters depending on the model. With a wired telephone, they were able to demonstrate two-way interception. They could hear not only the sound from the speakers but also the potential victim’s speech, which the headset’s built-in microphone and analog-to-digital converter had captured.
Advantages and limitations of the method
Any attack that requires getting very close to the target is challenging by definition. The need to tune the frequency of the “amplifying” radio signal for each specific device makes the attack even harder. In their experiments, the researchers had to use frequencies from one to eight megahertz.
Despite these caveats, the main achievement of this attack is its being able to target the quirks of the analog components in an electronic device. These components inherently produce stray emissions, and there’s almost no way to reduce them.
Similar surveillance methods that intercept a digital signal can be stopped by adding a layer of encryption. When it comes to the analog side of a device, protecting the signal itself is much harder. Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw

News

Oct 13, 20264 mins

A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks.

Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages.

The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

The issue is now fixed, Bloom Security researcher Golan Myers told CSO. “The npm team confirmed that a fix had been shipped on October 2, introducing a 48-hour expiry for unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations,” he said.

Myers said Bloom has not observed active exploitation in the wild, but confirmed that the flaw was successfully used to publish a new version of an existing npm package under their own controlled testing conditions. The fix addresses the exposure associated with unvalidated configurations, although maintainers still need to review their existing trust relationships, Bloom wrote in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Tuesday.

A reclaimed repository name enabled package publishing

npm’s Trusted Publishing allows package maintainers to publish releases through automated workflows using OpenID Connect (OIDC), avoiding long-lived publishing credentials. However, Bloom found that npm’s trust configuration relied on the GitHub repository’s owner/repository name instead of its immutable repository ID.

When a repository is renamed, transferred, or deleted, its former name may become available for another user to claim. An attacker could create a repository at that address and configure a GitHub Actions workflow with the expected filename. Because npm checked the repository name and workflow filename without verifying the permanent repository ID, the attacker could potentially obtain a valid publishing credential for a package they did not own.

The researchers demonstrated the attack against a researcher-controlled package, publishing a new version from a GitHub repository belonging to a different organization. The attack did not require compromising the legitimate maintainer’s GitHub or npm account or stealing their credentials.

Their registry-wide scan identified more than 1500 vulnerable packages with over 10 million combined downloads and more than one million downloads per month. One package accounted for over 200,000 monthly downloads, according to Bloom.

AI agents amplify the supply-chain risk

Bloom argues that AI coding agents can accelerate the distribution of malicious dependencies because they increasingly select and install software packages with limited human intervention.

Across dozens of organizations, the researchers measured approximately 70 agent-installed packages per endpoint each month, rising to around 350 on developer machines. These figures cover direct installations and exclude transitive dependencies.

A malicious release could execute attacker-controlled code through an installation hook when developers or CI systems install the compromised package. AI agents could introduce such a dependency without a developer explicitly selecting it. “A hijacked package doesn’t need to find a developer anymore,” Myers said. “It only needs to be the package an agent chooses.”
